name: Mars 1M No. 1 and No. 2
short_status: Two spacecraft, two launch failures, on 10 and 14 October 1960. Neither reached Earth orbit, and the USSR never acknowledged either flight; almost everything known about them comes from Western tracking and from post-Soviet memoirs.
tagline: OKB-1 (USSR) · Soviet Union · Flyby · 1960 · The first attempts Failure
stats: Soviet attempt to send a spacecraft to another planet
each craft, carrying about 10 kg of instruments

facts.label: Launch, 1M No. 1
facts.value: 10 October 1960, 14:27:49 UTC (17:27 Moscow time), Molniya 8K78 vehicle L1-4M from Site 1 at NIIP-5, Tyuratam (Baikonur). This was the maiden flight of the 8K78.

facts.label: Launch, 1M No. 2
facts.value: 14 October 1960, 13:51:03 UTC (16:51 Moscow time), Molniya 8K78 vehicle L1-5M from the same pad, four days after the first.

facts.label: Launch vehicle
facts.value: 8K78, the four-stage development of Korolev's R-7 later named Molniya. These two launches were its first two flights. Both failed on the third stage, Blok I, before the fourth stage (Blok L) was ever reached.

facts.label: Who built it
facts.value: OKB-1 under chief designer Sergei Korolev, with Vadim Petrov as lead designer for the 1M spacecraft. Blocks were assembled at Factory No. 88; final assembly and testing happened at the launch range itself.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: About 650 kg each. NSSDCA lists 650 kg for No. 1 and 640 kg for No. 2; Perminov and Russian sources give 650 kg for both, and no source we found explains the 10 kg difference.

facts.label: Spacecraft design
facts.value: Near-identical to the Venera 1 design: a sealed cylindrical body about 2 m tall, two solar panel wings feeding silver-zinc batteries, a 2.33 m mesh high-gain antenna and a long antenna arm.

facts.label: Science payload
facts.value: About 10 kg: a boom-mounted magnetometer, a cosmic ray counter, a plasma ion trap, a radiometer, a micrometeorite detector, a spectroreflectometer for the CH band (then thought to be a possible marker of organic life), and a phototelevision camera in the sealed module shooting through a viewport.

facts.label: Instruments removed before launch
facts.value: On 3 October 1960 the State Commission voted to strip the phototelevision unit and Professor Lebedinsky's spectroreflectometer to recover mass as the launch slipped past the optimal date. Chertok records that the life detector was first tried out on the steppe near the pad, where it reported that there was no life at Tyuratam.

facts.label: Failure, 1M No. 1
facts.value: Control was lost on the third stage around T+300 to 310 seconds when the gyro horizon issued a false pitch command, most likely from a broken contact in its command potentiometer caused by vibration. The stage swung past seven degrees, a limit contact closed and the engine was shut down. Destruct followed at about T+324 seconds; the stack reached roughly 120 km and burned up over eastern Siberia.

facts.label: Failure, 1M No. 2
facts.value: A leak in a liquid oxygen line chilled the third stage's kerosene valve while the rocket still stood on the pad. The valve froze shut, so when the start command went out at about T+290 seconds the third stage engine never lit, and the vehicle burned up over Siberia.

facts.label: Intended arrival
facts.value: 1M No. 2 would have flown past Mars on 15 May 1961.

facts.label: Ground segment
facts.value: The deep space complex at Yevpatoria in Crimea (NIP-16, the Pluton complex) was declared ready to work these launches in October 1960. Its ADU-1000 arrays of eight 16 m dishes were mounted on steerable frames built from battleship gun turrets and railway bridge trusses.

facts.label: Public acknowledgement
facts.value: None at the time, and none for decades. NASA's Administrator told Congress in 1962 that the 10 October launch had been a Mars attempt; some Soviet scientists denied it. V. G. Perminov, later lead designer for Mars and Venus spacecraft at the Lavochkin bureau, confirmed in a 1999 NASA monograph that both October 1960 launches were Mars missions and were identical to each other.

facts.label: Names
facts.value: The Western press coined Marsnik 1 and Marsnik 2. NASA's catalogue lists them as Mars 1960A and Mars 1960B, and also as Korabl 4 and Korabl 5. The internal Soviet designations were simply 1M No. 1 and 1M No. 2; no public Soviet name was ever assigned.

timeline: Boris Chertok flies to Tyuratam as technical director for the spacecraft; Arkady Ostashev is his deputy.
An An-12 delivers two half-assembled 1M craft to the range. No. 1 goes straight to electrical testing, No. 2 into the vacuum chamber for a leak check.
At a technical management meeting the onboard radio complex is found to be simply inoperable. Its lead engineer asks for one more day; the request draws laughter.
Round-the-clock rework finally gets the team to a full integrated test. So many deviations appear that launch on the optimal date is judged impossible.
The phototelevision unit produces something resembling a test picture, to general jubilation, then fails on the repeat run.
The State Commission removes the camera and the life-detecting spectroreflectometer to save mass. Both craft will now fly with no way of photographing Mars.
The third anniversary of Sputnik is marked at the range with champagne sent by a French winemaker, a week after the optimal Mars date has already been missed.
Chertok releases 1M No. 1 for mating with the fourth stage and turns the whole team onto the backup craft, No. 2.
Launch at 14:27:49 UTC on the 8K78's maiden flight. The third stage's gyro horizon fails, the engine is cut, and the vehicle is destroyed at about T+324 seconds over eastern Siberia.
Launch at 13:51:03 UTC. A frozen kerosene valve on the third stage prevents ignition and the second Mars craft follows the first into the Siberian sky.
The date on which 1M No. 2 was to have flown past Mars.
V. G. Perminov's monograph, published by the NASA History Division, confirms from inside the Soviet programme that both October 1960 launches were Mars missions.

images.caption: A colour photograph of a four stage Molniya 8K78 launch vehicle being raised to the vertical by its erector at Baikonur, with the service gantries, cranes and flame trench around it. The source captions the frame 'Preparing to Launch the 1M Mars Probe, Oct 10, 1960'.
images.credit: Soviet state archive photograph, photographer unrecorded; reproduced by Don P. Mitchell, mentallandscape.com

images.caption: A full scale mockup of Venera 1 on display at the Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics in Moscow, showing the pressurised cylindrical body, the dome on top, the perforated solar panel and the furled mesh high gain antenna. Venera 1 was the 1VA vehicle, built a few months after the 1M and reusing as much of the 1M design as possible, with the dome added on top that the 1M did not carry.
images.credit: Armael, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons; Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics, Moscow

images.caption: A four stage launch vehicle of the R-7 family lying horizontal on its rail transporter erector under a grey sky, photographed on 12 August 2004 and identified by the photographer as a Molniya. The 1M probes were launched on the Molniya 8K78, which was brand new in October 1960.
